opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a genuinely positive development, at least in part, and it connects pretty directly to the argument I was making. My concern with the standard paradigm was that we'd take a pretrained model, fine-tune it on a large training set drawn from some benchmark, and then evaluate it on a test set sampled from exactly the same distribution. That setup rewards a model for picking up whatever statistical regularities happen to be present in that particular dataset, including the annotation artifacts and shortcuts that crowd workers inadvertently introduce. So you'd get very impressive numbers that didn't necessarily tell you much about whether the system had acquired the general ability the benchmark was supposed to measure.

Few-shot learning, at least in principle, removes a lot of that opportunity. If the model sees only a handful of examples, or just an instruction, it can't fit the idiosyncrasies of a specific dataset in the same way. That's much closer to how we'd evaluate a person: you don't give someone a hundred thousand labeled entailment pairs before asking them whether one sentence follows from another. So in that sense the field has moved toward the kind of evaluation I was advocating, where the model has to bring general competence to a task rather than learning the task's surface statistics.

That said, I'd add a few caveats. First, the problem hasn't disappeared so much as moved. With pretraining corpora this large, we often don't know what the model has seen, so the question of whether a test example is really out of distribution, or whether something very similar, or even the benchmark itself, was in the training data, becomes much harder to answer. Contamination is the new version of the identically distributed problem, and in some ways it's worse because it's opaque.

Second, few-shot performance can be surprisingly sensitive to the exact prompt, the choice and ordering of examples, and so on. That sensitivity is itself evidence that we're not always measuring a robust underlying ability. A system that has truly learned a generalization shouldn't flip its answer because you reformatted the demonstrations.

And third, I still think we need targeted, controlled evaluations — things like systematic generalization tests and carefully constructed challenge sets — that probe specific capacities, rather than relying on aggregate scores. Few-shot learning changes how the model is adapted to a task, but it doesn't by itself tell us what the model has learned. So I'd see it as a step in the right direction, but one that makes careful experimental design more important, not less.

r001.rationale: The response says same-distribution evaluation rewards models for exploiting benchmark-specific statistical regularities and annotation shortcuts.

r002.rationale: It says few-shot learning limits task-specific fitting and moves evaluation toward requiring general competence, addressing the concern about extensive fine-tuning.

r003.rationale: The response says large pretraining makes contamination harder to assess, but does not say that concern about how much training data models require is worsening.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a genuinely positive development, though with some important caveats. The core of my critique was that when you fine-tune a model on tens or hundreds of thousands of examples from a particular dataset and then test it on held-out examples from that same dataset, you're not really measuring whether the model has learned the task in the sense we care about. You're measuring whether it has picked up whatever statistical regularities happen to be in that dataset, including annotation artifacts and quirks of how the data was collected. Humans don't learn natural language inference from a hundred thousand labeled examples. If you give a person the instructions and a couple of examples, they do the task, and they do it in a way that generalizes to inputs that look nothing like what they've seen.

So few-shot learning moves us closer to that human-like setting. If the model only sees a handful of examples, it has much less opportunity to latch onto dataset-specific artifacts, and in principle what you're testing is something more like the model's prior understanding of the task. That's the right direction. It makes the evaluation setup look more like the thing we actually want to know about.

But I'd be cautious about a few things. First, few-shot learning doesn't eliminate the identically distributed problem, it just relocates it. The model has been pretrained on an enormous corpus, and we often don't know what's in it. If the test data, or data very much like it, appeared during pretraining, then the few-shot evaluation is contaminated in a way that's hard to detect. So in a sense the distribution question has moved from the fine-tuning set to the pretraining set, where it's much more opaque.

Second, we've learned that few-shot performance can be surprisingly sensitive to the specific examples you pick, their order, the exact phrasing of the prompt. That brittleness is itself a sign that the model may not be doing the task in a robust, generalizable way. A human doesn't fail at an inference task because you reordered the two demonstration examples.

And third, the way I'd put it is that the evaluation methodology should be tied to the scientific question. If the question is whether a system has acquired a genuine, generalizable competence, then what we need are tests specifically constructed to probe generalization: controlled challenge sets, out-of-distribution examples, cases designed to distinguish the right generalization from plausible shortcuts. Few-shot learning is compatible with that, and arguably makes it easier because you're not spending your evaluation budget on training data. But it doesn't automatically deliver it. You can still evaluate a few-shot model on an in-distribution benchmark and draw the same overly optimistic conclusions we were drawing before.

So the shift is welcome, but I'd see it as changing the conditions under which we should ask the question, rather than answering it.

r001.rationale: It says models tested on held-out examples from the same dataset can learn that dataset’s statistical regularities, including artifacts and collection quirks, rather than generalize.

r002.rationale: It says few-shot learning moves evaluation closer to the desired setting and reduces the opportunity to exploit dataset-specific artifacts, addressing the concern about extensive task-specific fine-tuning.

r003.rationale: It describes few-shot learning as a welcome shift away from large-scale task-specific fine-tuning; it does not say the concern about how much training data models require is worsening.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising shift, but it doesn’t automatically solve the evaluation problem. My concern with identically distributed evaluation is that a model can do very well on held-out examples by exploiting regularities that are specific to a dataset. If we train and test on the same distribution, it’s hard to tell whether it has learned something more general.

Few-shot learning changes that setup in an interesting way. If you give a model only a handful of examples, there’s less opportunity to learn all the quirks of a particular dataset. That makes it a potentially stronger test of whether the model can apply what it already knows to a new task. But the model has still been trained on an enormous amount of text, and we need to understand how the evaluation examples relate to that training experience. A task that’s new in the prompt isn’t necessarily new to the model.

So I’d separate the question of how many examples you need to specify a task from the question of how systematically you generalize. Few-shot performance tells us something important about the first. For the second, we still need evaluations where we deliberately change the distribution—for example, by testing combinations of familiar elements that weren’t available during learning. That’s where we can start distinguishing successful pattern matching from the kind of generalization we’re interested in.

r001.rationale: It says models can succeed on held-out examples by exploiting dataset-specific regularities when training and testing use the same distribution, which conveys reliance on dataset-specific correlations.

r002.rationale: It says few-shot learning leaves less opportunity to learn dataset quirks and can better test applying prior knowledge to a new task, addressing the concern about extensive task-specific fine-tuning while noting it is not a complete solution.

r003.rationale: It notes that models have been trained on enormous amounts of text, but does not say concern about the amount of training data they require is worsening.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are two somewhat separate issues. Few-shot learning changes how we specify the task to the model: instead of updating its parameters on a large labeled dataset, we give it a few examples in context. That’s an interesting change, but it doesn’t by itself address the problem with identically distributed evaluation.

If the examples in the prompt and the test examples all come from the same distribution, the model can still succeed by exploiting regularities that won’t hold elsewhere. So the question remains: what has it learned, and how does that generalize when we change something? If we’re interested in syntactic generalization, for example, we should test constructions or combinations that weren’t represented in the demonstrations, rather than just testing new sentences drawn from the same source.

There’s also a complication with these pretrained models: we often don’t know whether something is actually new to them. A task might be presented with only a few examples, but the model may have encountered many similar examples during pretraining. So I’m excited about few-shot learning as a capability, but I wouldn’t take strong performance on those benchmarks as sufficient evidence for the kind of generalization we’re interested in.

r001.rationale: The response says same-distribution examples let models exploit regularities that may not hold elsewhere, but it does not clearly identify dataset-specific correlations with labels.

r002.rationale: The response says few-shot learning does not by itself address the evaluation concern; it does not state that it would address the concern about extensive task-specific fine-tuning.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that concern about the amount of training data models require is worsening.
